summary: Complexity is widely used in network design, yet there is no generally accepted definition. Existing complexity metrics usually address only one aspect of a network. This informational document gives a framework for defining network complexity, with the aim of helping people talk about and compare it.

plainLanguage.summary: People say a network is complicated, but nobody agrees what that means. This offers a way to describe and compare how tangled a network is.

subtitle: Understanding and measuring complexity in network design.

tldr.problem: Network designers use the concept of complexity constantly, but there is no agreed-upon definition or way to measure it, making it difficult to compare design choices objectively.
tldr.mechanism: This document provides a framework identifying sources of complexity (state, algorithms, churn, hardware, knowledge) and showing how design trade-offs shift complexity between different areas.
tldr.outcome: The framework helps engineers understand where complexity hides in networks and guides researchers studying network complexity as a formal problem.

facts.label: Design philosophy
facts.value: Finding the simplest solution to solve a problem

facts.label: Key property
facts.value: Robust yet fragile: robust to random failures, fragile to targeted attacks

today: RFC 7980 is an Informational document that summarizes work by the IRTF Network Complexity Research Group at the time of its closure. It does not present final answers but rather a framework to guide future research. Engineers and researchers continue to grapple with network complexity measurement; the framework it provides remains useful for thinking through design trade-offs.

sections.title: The Problem of Undefined Complexity
sections.content:
Network design is fundamentally about finding the simplest solution to solve a problem. Yet there is no generally accepted definition of what makes a network complex. Engineers make design decisions based on rough estimates of complexity rather than solid understanding. This document, produced by the IRTF's Network Complexity Research Group before its closure in 2014, provides a framework to guide future research and help engineers recognize where complexity arises.

The document acknowledges that it may be impossible to define a single metric for overall network complexity. Instead, it provides conceptual tools for understanding complexity as a system-level property, not just a sum of component-level properties, and identifies key areas where complexity interacts with engineering decisions.
sections.plainLanguage: Engineers know complicated networks are hard to manage, but they do not have a good way to measure or compare how complex different designs are.

sections.title: What Complexity Is and Is Not
sections.content:
A complex network exhibits several behaviors: Self-Organization (protocols and processes run without external control, but their interaction can be unpredictable), Unpredictability (local changes can have surprising global effects), Emergence (the system as a whole behaves differently than the sum of its parts), Non-linearity (small inputs produce unexpectedly large results), and Fragility (a small break can crash the entire system).

The document distinguishes between complex and complicated. Complicated systems are deterministic and can be understood through analysis (like a 10,000-line configuration file that is tedious but understandable). Complex systems, by contrast, have emergent behaviors that cannot be fully predicted from their parts (like routing convergence behavior across a multi-vendor network). A system can be both complicated and complex.

Networks exhibit the Robust Yet Fragile property: the Internet is robust against single-component failures but fragile to coordinated attacks. All network designs make trade-offs among different design goals. The classic saying "Good, Fast, Cheap: Pick any two" reflects this reality across real network design.
sections.plainLanguage: Complex networks are unpredictable and can act in surprising ways. Complex is different from just being complicated. Networks are tough in some ways and weak in others.

sections.title: Design Trade-Offs
sections.content:
Network complexity is a system-level problem. To address it, engineers can treat components as black boxes with well-understood interfaces, or they can view design as a continuum of trade-offs where reducing complexity in one area adds it in another.

Control-Plane State versus Path Optimality: Every piece of information added to the control plane (more routing details, policy information, tunneling state) adds complexity to monitoring and troubleshooting. Removing information reduces complexity but forces traffic onto suboptimal paths. The network stretches (takes longer routes) to use less state.

Configuration Complexity versus Failure Domain Separation: Smaller failure domains (where a problem affects fewer devices) are desirable but require configuration complexity like route filters and metric modifications. Larger failure domains are simpler to configure but propagate failures more widely.

Policy Centralization versus Consistent Policy Application: Centralizing packet-marking or quality-of-service policies to one location reduces configuration management but means packets at the network edge are not marked correctly. Distributing policy to all edge devices ensures consistency but requires managing more devices.

Reactivity versus Stability: Fast detection of network changes can destabilize the control plane if too much change information is injected. Slowing change propagation through exponential backoff, dampening, and timers adds complexity but prevents oscillation and overload.
sections.plainLanguage: Designers face trade-offs: less routing info but worse paths, smaller failure impact but more configuration, centralized policy but inconsistent behavior, fast reaction but network instability. Each choice shifts complexity somewhere else.

sections.title: Elements and Location of Complexity
sections.content:
Complexity appears in different forms: Physical Network (devices, wiring, redundancy), Algorithms (protocols and their intrinsic complexity), State (routing tables, configuration, security), Churn (rate of change), and Knowledge (what operators must understand).

Complexity can be located in different places using the Complexity Cube: network elements (distributed algorithms running on every router), central systems (controllers, NOCs computing answers), or human operators (static configuration). The choice of location affects overall complexity.

Dependencies also create complexity. Local dependencies exist between nearby routers. Network-wide dependencies occur when a change in one region affects distant regions through routing feedback loops. External dependencies involve the application layer, transport protocols, and media, where incompatible choices at different layers (like error-correcting media plus TCP retransmission) can cause unexpected interactions.

Technical Debt accumulates when suboptimal decisions are made because the optimal solution is impossible at the time. Over decades, accumulated suboptimal changes create significant complexity that would not exist had the optimal solution been available.
sections.plainLanguage: Complexity hides in devices, algorithms, data, constant changes, and what people need to know. It can be spread across many routers, concentrated in one controller, or exist in what a human operator has to remember. Past mistakes also add up.

sections.title: Parameters for Measuring Complexity
sections.content:
When attempting to measure complexity, engineers should consider parameters including: State (control-plane state, forwarding state, configuration), Cost (capital and operating expenses), Bandwidth/Delay/Jitter (traffic characteristics), Configuration Complexity (ease of configuration and maintenance), Susceptibility to Denial of Service, Security (confidentiality and integrity), Scalability (how large can it grow), Stability (robustness to local change), Reactivity (convergence speed), Extensibility (can it handle new services), Troubleshooting Difficulty (how easy to find and fix problems), Per-Hop Forwarding Behavior (optimality), and Predictability (can you forecast the effect of a change).

These parameters interact in complex ways. Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) could serve as a proxy for complexity if calculated to include all factors, including staff training and troubleshooting time. However, there is no single threshold of acceptable complexity; different network types (enterprise, carrier, access, core) have different tolerance for complexity.
sections.plainLanguage: Complexity comes from many sources: how much data is stored, money to build and run it, traffic delays, how hard it is to set up, attack surface, security, size limits, stability, speed of change, future flexibility, diagnosis difficulty, path efficiency, and predictability.
